title: Termux: Linux on Your Phone
summary: A real Linux terminal on Android, no root needed.

pages.title: Install it the right way
pages.body:
Termux is a terminal app that gives you a Linux environment on Android. You can install thousands of packages: Python, Git, Nmap, and more.

Install it from F-Droid or Termux's official GitHub releases. The old Play Store version went without updates for a long time and often fails to install packages.

After first launch, refresh the package list:
$ pkg update && pkg upgrade

If it asks questions during the upgrade, press Enter to keep the default.
pages.tip: Termux is like renting a small room with a Linux workshop inside your phone.

pages.title: First commands
pages.body:
The LV.01 commands work right away here:
$ pwd
$ ls -a
$ mkdir practice && cd practice

To let Termux read your phone's Download folder:
$ termux-setup-storage
Once allowed, phone folders live in ~/storage/shared.

Install commonly used tools:
$ pkg install python git curl nano

Try creating a file and running Python:
$ echo "print('hello cipher')" > hello.py
$ python hello.py
pages.tip: Learning the terminal is like learning a manual car: awkward for a week, then it's habit.

pages.title: Using Termux safely
pages.body:
Termux is powerful, so be careful:
- Don't paste commands or scripts from random groups or videos without understanding them. "Hack WhatsApp" or "hack Facebook" scripts are almost always scams, or they steal your data
- Understand any command with rm -rf, curl ... | bash, or a password prompt before running it
- Termux runs with normal app permissions, but files you grant access to can be deleted or changed
- Type exit to leave, and if things get messy, clear the app's data to start fresh
pages.tip: A kitchen knife is a great tool. But don't accept a knife from a stranger who calls it a "magic knife".

quiz.prompt: The recommended source for installing Termux is...
quiz.explanation: The old Play Store version went unmaintained for a long time.

quiz.prompt: The first command after installing Termux should be...
quiz.explanation: It refreshes package lists and versions.

quiz.prompt: The command that lets Termux access phone folders is...
quiz.explanation: Once allowed, phone folders appear under ~/storage.

quiz.prompt: A video shows a "1-minute Termux WhatsApp hack script". You should...
options: Not run it; it's almost always a scam or data stealer
quiz.explanation: Such scripts often steal the account of whoever runs them.

quiz.prompt: The command to install Python in Termux?
quiz.explanation: pkg is Termux's package manager.

title: Nmap: Mapping Networks
summary: Finding devices and open ports on your own network.

pages.title: What Nmap is for
pages.body:
Nmap (Network Mapper) is the best-known network scanner. Admins use it for inventory and pentesters for active recon:
- Which devices are up on the network
- Which ports are open
- What services and versions run on those ports

Remember LV.04: scanning other people's networks or servers without permission is illegal. Practice only on your own home network, or on targets provided for practice.
pages.tip: Nmap is like walking around the neighborhood checking which doors are open. Fine at your own house; at others', it's suspicious.

pages.title: Your first scan
pages.body:
In Termux:
$ pkg install nmap

First find your router's IP in Toolbox → Network Info (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1). Then:
$ nmap 192.168.1.1

Find which devices are up in one subnet (the /24 from LV.01):
$ nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

See service versions on open ports:
$ nmap -sV 192.168.1.1

Nmap also offers an official practice target: scanme.nmap.org, which you may scan gently.
pages.tip: -sn is like taking a headcount at home without knocking on every door.

pages.title: Reading the results
pages.body:
Sample output:
| PORT    STATE  SERVICE
| 53/tcp  open   domain
| 80/tcp  open   http
| 443/tcp open   https

Meaning:
- open: a service is listening
- closed: reachable but nothing is listening
- filtered: blocked by a firewall, Nmap can't tell

A home router opening port 80 (its admin page) to the local network is normal. It's dangerous if the admin page is reachable from the internet. Make sure the router admin password has been changed.
pages.tip: Scan results are like a floor plan marking which doors are open, closed, or fenced off.

quiz.prompt: Where can you legally practice Nmap?
options: Your own home network or scanme.nmap.org
quiz.explanation: Scanning without permission can be illegal.

quiz.prompt: The Nmap option to find live devices without port scanning?
quiz.explanation: -sn = ping scan / host discovery.

quiz.prompt: A "filtered" port state means...
options: A firewall blocks it so Nmap can't be sure
quiz.explanation: The probe got no clear reply.

quiz.prompt: The -sV option is used to...
quiz.explanation: Service versions help find known flaws.

quiz.prompt: The notation 192.168.1.0/24 in Nmap scans...
quiz.explanation: Remember the subnet math from LV.01.

title: Wireshark & PCAPdroid
summary: Inspecting network packets from your own device to see HTTP vs HTTPS.

pages.title: Meet packet capture
pages.body:
Packet capture means recording packets passing through a network, then dissecting them. It's the most honest way to see what apps really send.

- Wireshark: the most popular desktop app (Windows, Mac, Linux) for packet analysis
- PCAPdroid: a no-root Android app that records your own phone's traffic through a local VPN, and can export .pcap files to open in Wireshark

Which app talks to which server, when, and how often all becomes visible.
pages.tip: Packet capture is like a CCTV on the street outside: you see whose cars pass, which way, and when.

pages.title: Practice: HTTP vs HTTPS
pages.body:
Try it in PCAPdroid:
- Start recording, open one http:// site (e.g. http://neverssl.com) and one https:// site
- Stop, then inspect the connections

In Wireshark, use filters to focus:
$ http
$ dns
$ tls
$ ip.addr == 192.168.1.1

HTTP packets are plainly readable: the page address, headers, even form contents. HTTPS packets only show the destination domain; the content is encrypted noise. Real proof of what LV.00 and LV.03 taught.
pages.tip: HTTP is a postcard, HTTPS a sealed envelope. Now you've seen the difference yourself.

pages.title: Ethics & privacy
pages.body:
Recording other people's traffic without permission is wiretapping and can be illegal. So:
- Record only your own devices and networks
- .pcap files may contain sensitive data (cookies, sites visited). Don't share them carelessly
- Stop recording when done, since PCAPdroid shows up as an active VPN

Everyday benefit: you can check whether a suspicious app quietly sends data to unknown servers.
pages.tip: Putting CCTV in your own house is fine. Putting it in someone else's room is a violation.

quiz.prompt: PCAPdroid records phone traffic without root by...
quiz.explanation: Traffic is routed through a local VPN on the phone itself.

quiz.prompt: The Wireshark filter to show only DNS queries?
quiz.explanation: Display filters match protocol names.

quiz.prompt: In a packet capture, an HTTPS site shows...
options: The destination domain, with encrypted content
quiz.explanation: The domain is still visible via SNI/DNS, but content is encrypted.

quiz.prompt: Recording a cafe's Wi-Fi traffic without permission is...
quiz.explanation: Record only your own devices and networks.

quiz.prompt: Why shouldn't .pcap files be shared carelessly?
options: They can contain sensitive data like cookies
The format is a state secret
quiz.explanation: Session cookies in a capture can be used to hijack accounts.

title: Burp Suite & Web Labs
summary: Intercepting web requests and practicing LV.02 flaws legally.

pages.title: An intercepting proxy
pages.body:
Burp Suite is the main tool for testing web apps. The Community edition is free for Windows, Mac, and Linux.

How it works: Burp sits as a proxy between the browser and the server. Each request pauses in Burp so you can view it, change it, and send it on.

Burp has a preconfigured built-in browser, so there's no manual proxy or certificate setup.
pages.tip: Burp is like a mail carrier you can tell to stop, open the envelope, change the letter, and deliver it. That's why it belongs only in a practice "post office".

pages.title: Features beginners use
pages.body:
- Proxy → Intercept: hold a request and see its method, headers, cookies, and body (recall LV.02)
- HTTP history: every request is logged
- Repeater: resend one request repeatedly while tweaking parameters, e.g. change id=1042 to id=1043 to test IDOR
- Decoder: encode/decode Base64, URL, hex (like Cipher's Hash tool)

Intruder is deliberately rate-limited in Community. That's enough for learning.
pages.tip: Repeater is like trying keys one by one in a practice lab, noting which ones open the door.

pages.title: Official practice grounds
pages.body:
PortSwigger (Burp's maker) runs the free Web Security Academy, with lessons plus hundreds of labs built to be attacked: SQL injection, XSS, access control, and more.

A good order:
- "Apprentice" SQL injection and XSS labs
- Access control / IDOR labs
- Then move up to Practitioner

Local alternatives: DVWA or OWASP Juice Shop, vulnerable apps you run on your own laptop.
pages.tip: A practice lab is a boxing gym: the opponent is there to be hit.

quiz.prompt: Burp Suite works as a...
options: Proxy between the browser and the server
quiz.explanation: Requests pause in Burp before going on.

quiz.prompt: The Burp feature to resend a request while tweaking parameters is...
quiz.explanation: Repeater suits testing IDOR or injection.

quiz.prompt: The free, legal place to practice Burp from its maker is...
quiz.explanation: Hundreds of labs are built to be attacked.

quiz.prompt: DVWA and OWASP Juice Shop are...
options: Vulnerable apps for practicing on your own laptop
quiz.explanation: Deliberately flawed for learning.

quiz.prompt: Why shouldn't Burp be used on random sites?
options: Altering requests to others' systems without permission is an illegal attack
quiz.explanation: The tool is legal; how you use it decides.

title: CyberChef & Online Tools
summary: A Swiss Army knife for data, plus safe ways to check files and links.

pages.title: CyberChef: a data kitchen
pages.body:
CyberChef is a free web app made by GCHQ (the UK intelligence agency), nicknamed the "cyber Swiss Army knife". You build a "recipe" of steps:
- From Base64 → From Hex → Gunzip
- Hashes, ROT13, XOR, extracting URLs or IPs from text
- Magic: auto-detects the encoding used

Everything runs in the browser; data isn't sent to a server. It can also be downloaded to use offline. Popular in CTF crypto and forensics challenges.
pages.tip: CyberChef is a kitchen: ingredients in on the left, the recipe in the middle, the dish out on the right.

pages.title: Checking suspicious files & links
pages.body:
- VirusTotal: scans files, links, or hashes with dozens of antivirus engines at once
- urlscan.io: opens a link on their servers and shows a screenshot and where it leads
- haveibeenpwned.com: checks whether your email has leaked

Important about VirusTotal: uploaded files can be accessed by the security community. Don't upload personal documents or work secrets. To just check, search by the file's SHA-256 hash first (computable in Cipher's Hash tool).
pages.tip: Checking a link on urlscan is like sending a courier to photograph the address before you go yourself.

pages.title: Practice: crack a CTF flag
pages.body:
Cipher hides a Base64-encoded flag (see the hint in Mini CTF). Try cracking it with CyberChef:
- Open CyberChef in a browser
- Paste the Base64 text into the Input box
- Drag the "From Base64" operation into the Recipe
- Read the Output

Or click the magic wand (Magic) and let CyberChef guess. Once you have it, enter the flag in Mini CTF.
pages.tip: Like a puzzle in a workbook: the answer is there, you just need the right tool.

quiz.prompt: CyberChef is best for...
options: Transforming and decoding data with step recipes
quiz.explanation: Encoding, decoding, hashing, and data extraction.

quiz.prompt: Why not upload personal documents to VirusTotal?
options: Uploaded files can be accessed by the security community
quiz.explanation: Search by hash first if you only want to check.

quiz.prompt: The service that opens a link on its servers and shows a screenshot is...
quiz.explanation: You see where a link leads without opening it yourself.

quiz.prompt: The CyberChef operation that auto-guesses encodings is...
quiz.explanation: The magic wand icon.

quiz.prompt: Data you process in CyberChef is...
quiz.explanation: CyberChef runs entirely client-side.

title: Kali Linux & Practice Labs
summary: Build your own lab and start a guided practice path.

pages.title: Meet Kali Linux
pages.body:
Kali Linux is a Linux distro packed with hundreds of security tools: Nmap, Wireshark, Burp, John the Ripper, and more.

Kali isn't meant for daily use, and using Kali doesn't automatically make you skilled. The foundations still matter: networking, Linux, web, and the reasoning from earlier levels.

The safest way to start is running it inside your current laptop, not wiping Windows.
pages.tip: Kali is a complete toolbox. But an expensive toolbox doesn't make someone a mechanic overnight.

pages.title: How to run it
pages.body:
Three options on a Windows laptop:
- WSL (lightest). In PowerShell as admin:
$ wsl --install -d kali-linux
- VirtualBox or VMware: download the official VM image from kali.org, import it, and run. Give it at least 2–4 GB RAM
- Live USB: boot from a flash drive without touching the hard drive

Once inside, always update first:
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade

Download Kali only from kali.org. Images from other sites may be tampered with.
pages.tip: A virtual machine is a house inside a house: making a mess inside doesn't mess up the main house.

pages.title: A guided practice path
pages.body:
Legal, beginner-friendly practice platforms:
- TryHackMe: guided "rooms", many free. Start with Pre Security, then Cyber Security 101
- Hack The Box: tougher practice machines, with a Starting Point path
- PicoCTF: a beginner CTF from Carnegie Mellon, great for students
- OverTheWire Bandit: Linux command practice over SSH, level by level

Aim for 30 minutes a day, log each finished room on GitHub, and you've got a portfolio.
pages.tip: Like a game that levels up: every room you finish is XP for your career.

quiz.prompt: Kali Linux is...
options: A Linux distro with hundreds of security tools
quiz.explanation: A ready-made set of security testing tools.

quiz.prompt: The lightest way to run Kali on Windows?
quiz.explanation: WSL runs Linux alongside Windows.

quiz.prompt: Kali images should be downloaded from...
quiz.explanation: Other sources may carry tampered images.

quiz.prompt: The beginner platform with guided "rooms" is...
quiz.explanation: Many free rooms, great for starting out.

quiz.prompt: Why doesn't using Kali automatically make you skilled?
options: Tools are just tools; networking, Linux, and web basics are key
quiz.explanation: Understanding the basics is what makes tools useful.
